title: U.S. Army Unit Offers Soldiers a 4-Day Pass to Play GTA VI as Reenlistment Perk
excerpt: A memo from the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion offering leave to play the most anticipated game of 2026 has gone viral online.
body:
• A memo circulating online shows a U.S. Army battalion offering soldiers a special 4-day pass to play Grand Theft Auto VI as an incentive to reenlist
  • The offer comes from the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion and has gone viral, highlighting the creative lengths military units go to for retention
  • GTA VI, set to release November 19 at $79.99, has generated unprecedented pre-order demand with nearly 90% of orders going to the pricier Ultimate Edition

The U.S. Army has tried cash bonuses, station-of-choice assignments, and education benefits to keep soldiers in uniform. Now, at least one unit is trying something different: four days off to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

A memo circulating online this week appears to show the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion offering reenlisting soldiers a special 4-day pass timed to the launch of Rockstar Games' highly anticipated GTA VI, which releases on November 19. The image of the memo went viral on social media and gaming forums, drawing a mix of amusement, disbelief, and admiration for the battalion's unorthodox approach to retention.

When Gaming Meets Military Retention

The offer is unconventional, but it reflects a real challenge facing the U.S. military. Retention has been a persistent concern across all branches, with the Army in particular experimenting with creative incentives beyond traditional bonuses. In recent years, the service has offered station-of-choice assignments, training opportunities, and flexible career options to keep soldiers from walking when their contracts expire.

A 4-day pass — essentially a long weekend — is a relatively low-cost incentive. But for soldiers stationed at remote posts or those pulling demanding schedules, the appeal of guaranteed time off aligned with the biggest game launch in years is real. Military culture and gaming culture have long overlapped, and commanding officers who understand that connection have found it can be a powerful motivator.

The authenticity of the memo has not been officially confirmed by the Army, and units sometimes circulate such offers informally. But the concept itself is not unprecedented. Military personnel have conducted reenlistment ceremonies at GameStop locations and aboard aircraft carriers, and commanders have wide latitude to offer creative perks as long as they fall within regulations.

The Game Everyone Is Waiting For

Grand Theft Auto VI is arguably the most anticipated video game release of the decade. Set in the fictional state of Leonida — Rockstar's take on Florida — it features two protagonists, Jason and Lucia, and promises the studio's largest open world to date. The game has been in development for over 11 years.

Pre-order demand has been staggering. According to analytics firm Sensor Tower, nearly 90% of GTA VI pre-orders are for the $99.99 Ultimate Edition rather than the $79.99 standard version — a split the firm says is unlike anything it has seen before. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick confirmed the premium edition is "skewing more" in pre-order data.

Rockstar announced that an extended look at the game will premiere on Netflix on August 27 before launching on YouTube. The original trailer broke the YouTube record for most views in 24 hours for a non-music video.

A Lighter Side of Service

The story has resonated across social media precisely because it captures a familiar tension: the grinding reality of military life meeting a moment of pure pop-culture anticipation. For soldiers who have spent months in training rotations or deployments, the promise of a few uninterrupted days with the biggest game of the year is not trivial — it is a small but meaningful acknowledgment of what they care about outside of the uniform.

Whether or not this particular memo is official policy, it has already succeeded at something the Army spends millions trying to achieve: making reenlistment feel like it comes with something worth getting excited about.
